orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, still telling her story to Lockwood. She jumps forward twelve years: scholars date the main events of this chapter to the summer of 1797, when Edgar's daughter Cathy is thirteen and growing up at Thrushcross Grange.

notes.g: Lockwood reminds us that Nelly (Mrs. Dean) is still telling the story.
That gloomy time (the deaths told in Chapter XVII).
She grew fast and straight, like a larch tree.
notes.n: Larches are quick-growing conifers often planted on country estates.

notes.t: before the heath blossomed a second time over Mrs. Linton’s dust
notes.g: Before the heather had flowered twice over her mother's grave: in her second summer.
notes.n: Heather blooms purple in late summer. Catherine's grave is in a corner where the moor creeps over the churchyard wall (Chapter XVI).

notes.g: The dark eyes of her mother's family.
notes.n: Keep these eyes in mind.

notes.t: the Lintons’ fair skin and small features
notes.g: The pale skin and delicate face of her father's family.

notes.t: Her spirit was high, though not rough
notes.g: She was lively and bold, but not wild.

notes.m: Nothing to do with having qualifications. To 'qualify' something meant to moderate it.

notes.g: Faults that set off her good qualities.
notes.n: A 'foil' is something that makes another thing stand out by contrast.

notes.t: He took her education entirely on himself
notes.n: A gentleman's daughter would usually have had a governess or gone to a girls' school.

notes.t: beyond the range of the park
notes.g: Outside the grounds of the Grange.

notes.t: Gimmerton was an unsubstantial name in her ears
notes.g: The village was just a name to her, not a real place.

notes.n: A chapel was a small church serving an outlying area. Catherine's grave is in its churchyard.

notes.g: Someone completely shut away from the world.
A high rocky outcrop on the moors beyond Wuthering Heights.
notes.n: In her delirium in Chapter XII, Catherine imagined she was in the fairy cave under Penistone Crags.

notes.g: The steep drop; the cliff face.
Feed even a small, scrubby tree.

notes.t: that black hollow on the north-east side
notes.g: A shaded dip in the rocks where the sun never reaches.

notes.t: the brow of that tallest point
notes.g: The top edge of that highest hill.
A cave under Penistone Crags with local fairy legends.
notes.n: Catherine imagined herself there in Chapter XII.

notes.g: Counted every month as she grew older.

notes.t: Edgar had not the heart to pass it
notes.g: Edgar couldn't bear to go past Wuthering Heights.

notes.t: I said Mrs. Heathcliff lived above a dozen years
notes.g: Here 'Mrs. Heathcliff' is Isabella, who lived more than twelve years.
notes.n: Nelly said in Chapter XVII that Isabella died about thirteen years after Catherine.

notes.t: a kind of fever, slow at its commencement, but incurable
notes.g: A slow fever that grew worse until it killed.
notes.n: Probably consumption (tuberculosis), the great killer of the age. It was called consumption because it seemed to 'consume' the body.
'Adieu' is French for goodbye.

notes.t: deliver Linton safely into his hands
notes.g: Hand her son over to Edgar.
notes.n: Here 'Linton' is Isabella's son, Heathcliff's child, now about twelve. 'His hands' are Edgar's.

notes.t: assume the burden of his maintenance or education
notes.g: Take on the cost of keeping and schooling him.

notes.t: commending Catherine to my peculiar vigilance
notes.g: Putting Cathy in my special care.
notes.m: 'Peculiar' here means particular or special, not odd.

notes.n: 'Tea' was a light meal in the late afternoon or early evening.

notes.g: Her going beyond the allowed limits.

notes.t: an Arabian merchant, going to cross the Desert with his caravan
notes.g: A trader crossing the desert with a train of camels.
notes.n: Cathy is playing at stories like the Arabian Nights, popular in English translation since the early 1700s.
Pointers freeze and aim their noses at hidden game birds.

notes.g: A thin, see-through veil to keep off the sun.
A farm worker paid by the day.

notes.m: Not a large farm or estate worked by slaves. On an English estate it meant an area of planted trees.

notes.g: A thin, bendy stick cut from a hazel bush, used as a riding whip.

notes.n: Galloways were small, sturdy horses from south-west Scotland.

notes.m: 'Directly' meant immediately, not 'in a straight line'.
To 'ejaculate' meant to cry out suddenly.

notes.g: As fast as if I'd made a bet on it.
Climbing awkwardly, using hands and feet.

notes.n: Nelly doesn't name her here.

notes.t: since the death of Mr. Earnshaw
notes.g: Since Hindley's death, told in Chapter XVII.

notes.t: Step in and rest you a bit
notes.g: Come in and rest a while.

notes.n: An echo of the lost sheep in Jesus's parable (Luke 15).

notes.t: a great, strong lad of eighteen
notes.g: A big, strong young man of eighteen.
notes.n: This is Hareton, Hindley's son, who lost everything to Heathcliff at the end of Chapter XVII.

notes.t: concealing my joy under an angry countenance
notes.g: Hiding my joy behind an angry face.
She would gladly have ridden on.

notes.n: 'Wax' means grow, as the moon waxes.

notes.t: though they were just his own
notes.g: Her eyes were exactly like his.
notes.n: Both have the dark Earnshaw eyes: Cathy's mother and Hareton's father were sister and brother.

notes.g: A servant would call a young lady 'Miss'.
notes.n: Cathy assumes Hareton is either the owner's son or a servant, and he doesn't behave like a servant.

notes.g: Her relative, though she doesn't know it.

notes.t: the goblin-hunter rises in the marsh
notes.n: Flickering lights over marshes (will-o'-the-wisps) were often explained as goblins or spirits. Hareton has evidently told her some local tale.
Hareton's local word.

notes.t: I’ll see thee damned before I be thy servant
notes.g: I'd rather see you in hell than be your servant!
notes.n: 'Thee' and 'thy' were the familiar forms, used in Yorkshire to family, friends and inferiors. From a farm lad to a young lady, it is very rude.

notes.t: Nice words to be used to a young lady
notes.g: Fine language to use to a young lady (said ironically).
Hareton's father was the brother of Cathy's mother.
notes.n: Cathy has never been told about her mother's family at the Heights.

notes.t: Papa is gone to fetch my cousin from London
notes.g: Her other cousin, Linton, Isabella's son.
notes.n: This cousin is related through Cathy's father: Isabella was Edgar's sister. Isabella had been living near London.

notes.g: The son of a gentleman, not a farmhand.
notes.n: Class mattered enormously. Cathy is shocked that a rough worker could be family.

notes.m: Not a circus clown. A 'clown' was a rough, uneducated rustic.

notes.g: What each of them let slip.
The coming arrival of Isabella's son, whom Edgar is bringing home.
Mentioned by the first of the two: Cathy.
What the second one, the housekeeper, claimed.
To win her over; to make peace.
A good terrier puppy with short, bent legs.
notes.n: A 'whelp' is a puppy.

notes.t: bid her whist! for he meant nought
notes.g: Told her to hush, because he meant no harm.
notes.n: 'Whist' is an old word for hush; 'nought' is nothing.

notes.t: this antipathy to the poor fellow
notes.g: This dislike of the poor lad.

notes.t: attired in garments befitting his daily occupations
notes.g: Dressed in clothes suited to his everyday work.

notes.t: lounging among the moors after rabbits and game
notes.g: Roaming the moors hunting rabbits and wild birds.
notes.n: 'Game' means wild animals and birds hunted for food or sport, such as grouse.

notes.g: Face, read as a sign of character.
notes.n: Reading people's characters from their faces was a popular pseudo-science at the time.
Nelly's garden image: Hareton's good qualities are choked by neglect, but the 'soil' is rich.

notes.t: whose rankness far over-topped their neglected growth
notes.g: Whose wild, coarse growth far outgrew them.

notes.t: the timid susceptibility that would have given zest to ill-treatment
notes.g: The shy sensitivity that would have made bullying him enjoyable.

notes.t: bent his malevolence on making him a brute
notes.g: Set his ill will on turning him into a savage.

notes.t: he was never taught to read or write
notes.n: Remember Hareton's father went to college (Chapter V). The heir of an old landowning family would normally be educated.

notes.g: A single rule of good conduct.

notes.t: the head of the old family
notes.g: The heir of the Earnshaws, who had owned the Heights for centuries.
notes.n: Remember the name 'Hareton Earnshaw' and the date 1500 carved over the door (Chapter I).

notes.t: putting the master past his patience

notes.n: Probably from 'offal', meaning waste or rubbish.

notes.g: Heathcliff, who took over Hareton's inheritance.
Badly; in a way that deserved blame.

notes.t: Hareton’s blood would be required at his hands
notes.g: Heathcliff would answer to God for Hareton's ruin.
notes.n: From Ezekiel 3:18, where God warns that if a wicked man is not warned and dies in his sin, 'his blood will I require at thine hand'.

notes.t: instilled into him a pride of name, and of his lineage
notes.g: Taught him to be proud of his family name and ancestry.
Was almost superstitious, as if Heathcliff had unnatural powers.
Private curses, calling down God's anger.
notes.n: The Book of Common Prayer has a 'Commination' service that lists God's judgements against sinners.

notes.m: 'Near' meant tight-fisted, not close by. Nelly said the same in Chapter IV.

notes.t: a cruel hard landlord to his tenants
notes.g: A harsh landlord to the farmers who rent land from him.

notes.t: its ancient aspect of comfort under female management
notes.g: Its old comfortable look, now that a woman runs the house.

notes.t: the scenes of riot common in Hindley’s time
notes.g: The drunken chaos of Hindley's days.
The puppy Hareton gave her to make up.

notes.m: 'Smart' here means brisk and painful, not clever.

notes.g: Being out of favour with her.
The woman who opened the door at the Heights.

notes.t: the language he had held to her rankled in her heart
notes.g: The way he had spoken to her kept hurting.

notes.t: lay the grievance before her father
